A separate partition or volume doesn't really have as many benefits today as it once had. Most files systems are robust enough to not loose all your files during a crash, so separating out "dangerous" volatile files makes less sense. "/tmp" and log files on "/var" would make more changes to a file system, possibly during a crash. Not much of a problem today. There was also an issue with memory, but with gigabytes being standard, keeping many many file names and directories in memory is about expected. The built in disk cache and newer files systems should put memory to good use. Today, file access should be just about as fast if the file system is full or empty.
As for putting things on a separate disk however. The boot filesystem is nice to have on a solid state drive, faster boot and faster program start. Music, video, any media really, takes up much more space and faster access doesn't improve much, just has to be faster than the bitrate.

I know this doesn't directly answer your question, but maybe you'll find it helpful.

For your standard run of the mill desktop Linux system there's really no need to manually partition anything. Most of the time the default partitioning scheme is perfectly fine for whatever you're going to do. If you're going to do anything, opt to use LVM (Logical Volume Management) during the install. LVM will give you a bit of flexibility in the future if you choose to add new drives, or decide that you really do need segmented filesystems.

In the past you might have wanted to create new partitions to mitigate a potential partition corruption, or to make sure that a rouge program didn't start to fill up your hard drive by writing files to "/tmp". Now-a-days partition corruption really isn't an issue, and I've never had a program start recklessly filling up drive space.

On my main laptop I have:

120G SSD
- 500MB /boot (EXT4)
- 1G (SWAP0
- 118.5G / (LVM)

1TB HDD (btrfs)
SV1 /mnt/media
SV2 /mnt/backup

Everything on the 1TB hard drive shares the 1TB of space. The only reason I've broken it down into sub-volumes is to keep things organized, and it gives me some flexibility with unused (by me) btrfs features.

The "/boot" and SWAP partitions were created by Linux Mint during the install (default settings). I added the 1TB drive afterwards. If they had both been the same type of drive (e.g. both of them were SSDs) I would have added the 1TB to "/" through LVM.

Back when I was dual booting I just split the drive in half, put Linux on one and Windows on the other. It doesn't matter where you put either. The easiest way is to install Windows first. During the install use the disk partitioner to select 1/2 the drive to install to. Then install Linux and select the remaining unused space. Linux will figure out that Windows is there and most distros will set up grub (boot loader) options for you. If you ever need to adjust the space for each OS, boot a live CD that has Gparted on it and just resize the partitions. I've never had an issue with that going wrong, but as always back things up first.

You may run into a problem where (out of the blue) you can't boot into linux or windows or your bootloader says there's no OS. Don't panic. Boot to a live CD and re-install grub. 90% of the time the above issue is caused because Windows tried to repair the boot sector and screwed things up.

If you only need Windows for backwards compatibility (i.e. you're not going to be gaming or using specialized hardware) I highly recommend just installing Windows in a virtual machine. This saves a bit of duel booting hassle, and lets you run Linux and Windows at the same time.
